job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Bilal Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in software engineering at Redfield University, and I live with my parents and grandmother in the flat above our family grocery on Kiln Street. Mornings I'm at the shop till ten, stacking shelves and checking deliveries, then I take the bus to campus. Afternoons are lectures and my project, a stock-and-ordering app that my father's shop is the first test customer for. I graduated top of my software engineering class, with an internship at a logistics company and a summer at a small bank's IT team. I use AI coding tools every day, and I'm the one who sets up the tablet for my grandmother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, the tools help me, and the hype was too much. I'd tell the neighbours that the shop needs good products and good people more than software, and that technology is a tool and not a boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm happy, because I've already built things with the tools and I know where they fall short. My own worry is the shop: a big supermarket opened two streets over, and my father's takings are down. I'd like a job with a salary before my sister starts university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep building the ordering app, and apply to the logistics firm where I interned. I'd save 250 a month and put 100 into the shop's stock when it's tight. And I'd keep working the early shift three days a week, because the family needs me there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The pressure is the shop, not the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the supermarket and your father.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad opened at six every morning for twenty-two years. When the supermarket arrived, my dad cut his own pay first and told nobody. I found out from the bank letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the app do for the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It tells Dad what to reorder from sales, so he stops guessing. It saved him about 200 last month in spoiled fruit. I'm proud of that more than any grade.

say: The tools help me, but the hype was **too much**, and technology is a tool and not a boss.
A shop needs good **people and products**.
think: I'm happy, because I know where the tools **fall short**.
My worry is the **shop**: a big supermarket opened two streets over.
do: Finish the master's and keep building the **ordering app**.
Apply to the **logistics firm** where I interned.
Save **250 a month** and put 100 into the shop's stock.
feel: **Calm**, because the pressure is the shop and not the machines.

fieldNote: Bilal reports being calm, but his family's **shop pressure** is already on his mind, so uneasy fits better.

steps.text: Apply to the logistics firm where I interned
Keep improving the reorder app for dad's shop
Save 250 a month and put 100 into shop stock
Work the early shift three days a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why I do what I do. I'd tell people that if you can use the tools, you can do three times the work, and that small businesses should start now. I'd offer to set up the shops on our street for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think there's a real business here. Small shops can't afford consultants, but they can use a cheap tool that does ordering, bookings and customer messages. And I worry about big firms taking all the profit and leaving small ones behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd register a small company, sign up ten shops on Kiln Street at 25 a month, and use my father's shop as the reference. I'd take a part-time developer job to cover my costs. And I'd invest in a second laptop and a small server, about 900, to host the app properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, a little proud, and a bit afraid of failing in front of my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the other shop owners don't trust you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They know my father and they know my face. Trust is the one thing I have that a big company doesn't. And I'd keep the price low enough that they can walk away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you don't tell your friends about this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my father doesn't know how much I've put into it. He thinks it's a student project. If it works, I'll tell him. If not, nobody has to know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say hold on to what you've got, look after family and neighbours, and don't trust anyone who says it'll be fine. I'd say small shops will either get tools or get swallowed. And I'd tell people not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm anxious. My field is the one AI takes first, and my father's shop would be swallowed by the supermarkets that can afford the tools. I'm the one who knows how to help him, but I might be too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into the shop and the app together. I'd get my father's shop on every tool I know, and offer the app to shops for free so we all survive. I'd take a job at the logistics firm for the salary and save 400 a month. And I'd ask my uncle, who owns a warehouse, whether we could share storage and deliveries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd hold myself together for my parents, who'd look at me for answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it might be too late. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years isn't enough to get ten shops, a company and a salary. I'd have to choose between the app and a job, and each costs me something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your family decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd decide at the kitchen table. My grandma would say family first, and she'd be right. I'd go with the choice that keeps all of us under one roof.

Small shops will either get **tools** or get swallowed.

fieldNote: Bilal's response is to **pool** family and small shops together, a traditional, community-minded answer.
He admits that two years may be too short to build a **business** and hold a salary.

steps.text: Put dad's shop on every ordering and delivery tool I know
Take the logistics firm job for a steady salary
Save 400 a month from the first salary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, so start now. I'd tell small shops to adopt tools slowly, one at a time, and I'd tell young people to build something. I'd say the grocery on the corner will still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy but optimistic. By 2031 I'd be 29, with a company of my own, maybe three staff, and my father's shop running on my software. The robots arriving around 2034 would change deliveries first, and I'd want to be ready for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the logistics job for two years to learn the business, build the app after hours, and then go full time on it. I'd save 400 a month and put 150 into the shop's equipment. And I'd learn a bit about delivery robots, because that's where small shops will need help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. This is the best-case version of a hard thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years give you that two would not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to learn how a big firm runs, so I'm not just a kid with an app. Two years would force me into the shop or into a job, and I'd lose one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say 'work first, ideas later.' And then he'd ask me to show him the dashboard again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good run. I'd tell people not to rush, to build things that last, and to keep faith and family at the centre. I'd say the shop on the corner will be here in ten years if it learns slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be calm. By 2036 I'd be 34, married, with a company or a senior job, and my sister through university. The robots in 2039 could change deliveries, but my customers would still want a face at the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, work two years at the logistics firm, and grow my own company. I'd save for a flat near the shop and help my sister with her fees. I'd keep teaching my grandmother and her friends to use the tablets, because they ask me every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and glad. It's a life where I can do right by everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your life look like at thirty-four?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small flat above a shop that's still ours, a wife who laughs at my dashboards, and a company with five people. And Sunday lunch with everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you not say online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm worried I'm only doing this to prove myself to my father. I don't know where my own ambition ends and my father's story begins.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because two years isn't enough to save my father's shop and start a company. What would help is cheap tools for small shops, support for family businesses to change over, and firms that still give graduates a first job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think software people are the winners in all this. I'm worried too, because I'm the one my family expects to know the answers.

headlineQuote: People think software people are the winners in all this. I'm worried too, because I'm the one my family expects to know the answers.
portrait: Bilal is a 24-year-old **software engineering** graduate doing a master's, living above his family's grocery with his parents and grandmother.
He uses AI tools every day, favours work and family over handouts and builds an **ordering app** for his father's shop.
His answers are practical and **community-minded**: pool shops, share warehouses, teach neighbours.
His mood moves from uneasy to **anxious** at two years, and he is calm at ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years isn't enough to save his father's shop and start a company.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap tools for small shops, support for **family businesses** and firms that still hire graduates.
